summary: A 1975 description of the internal states of an NCP connection in the TENEX implementation, drawn as a finite state machine.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 689 describes how TENEX version 1.33 tracks an NCP connection from creation through data transfer and closing. Each state determines what the system does when an event occurs.

questions: what states does the tenex ncp use
how does an ncp connection close
subtitle: The connection-state machine used by the TENEX NCP implementation.

tldr.problem: An NCP must respond differently to connection events depending on whether a socket is free, listening, open, or closing.
tldr.mechanism: The memo documents the states, events, and actions in TENEX version 1.33, including how it handles incoming requests, closes, and timeouts.
tldr.outcome: It records the state machine used to implement the ARPANET Host-to-Host Protocol in that TENEX version.

today: RFC 689 describes the TENEX NCP implementation documented in 1975. The memo says it updates an earlier TENEX memo's finite-state-machine description.

sections.title: Connection States
sections.content:
The memo lists states including FREE, CLOSED, PENDING, LISTENING, RFC SENT, OPEN, and several closing and acknowledgement-wait states. A connection enters the OPEN state after the two sides have exchanged matching requests; data can then be transferred.

The diagrams distinguish a program-level close from a Host-to-Host protocol close. These can happen at different times, so closing may pass through intermediate states.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection moves through named stages, from unused to open and then closed. Some stages wait for the other computer or for outstanding data to finish.

sections.title: Events, Actions, and Timeouts
sections.content:
Events include incoming connection requests, local or remote close actions, acceptance, and timeout. For each event in each state, the state machine specifies an action and a next state. An event not expected in a state produces an error action.

The timeout is generally two minutes, except that error states are advanced more quickly and listening states do not time out. In the OPEN state, a timeout can trigger allocation resynchronization when the other host supports that extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The same event can require different actions at different stages. A timeout can move a stalled connection along, but a listening socket keeps waiting.

sections.title: Closing Without Losing Outstanding Data
sections.content:
When a local program closes a sending connection, the implementation waits for the final RFNM acknowledgement before sending a close command. When data is still outstanding after a remote close, the state machine waits for the final acknowledgement before completing cleanup.

The connection is not freed until required close messages and outstanding acknowledgements have been handled, or the relevant timeout path is taken.
sections.plainLanguage: Closing a connection does not always happen at once. The system may wait for the last data acknowledgement before it finishes closing and reuses the socket.
